title: Why Students Feel They Don’t Belong in the English Classroom
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles argues that English has lost students because what they are made to do in lessons no longer lets them belong to the subject. He opens with an extended comparison to feeling out of place in Los Angeles, then points to English falling from the most popular A level until 2012 to twelfth by 2022. He blames GCSE design and a decade of well-meant but inefficient teaching methods for a diet of quote exploders, PEE-style paragraphs, annotation, extracts, exam-question methods and writing by numbers. Against this he lists what students ought to learn: crafting and redrafting real stories, writing poems, reading aloud, sustained essays, debate, speeches and personal anthologies. His one-sentence summary is that we no longer teach students to be students of English, and he closes with a thought experiment asking readers to design ten tasks that would show real excellence.
points: Entries to English A level fell from first place to twelfth between 2012 and 2022, and Salles says students leave because the subject feels pointless or boring.
Common classroom routines such as mnemonic paragraphs, annotation and extract-based assessment train exam technique rather than membership of a community of readers and writers.
A good curriculum is defined by what students do, not just what they read, so loving attention to text choice is not enough.
He lists authentic tasks such as redrafting, reading poems aloud, long essays and debates that would let students develop a voice.
The closing exercise of writing ten tasks that would demonstrate real excellence exposes the gap between ideal and actual curriculum.
quotes: English was once the most inclusive and popular A level. Every year, until 2012, it was the number one choice. By 2022, it was the 12th most popular. The missing students now choose sociology and psychology. They aren’t fleeing because they want a STEM subject, employability or higher pay. They’re leaving in droves because for most English is either pointless, boring or both.

We’ve been herded that way by the artificiality and sheer lack of intellectual thought in the creation of the GCSE. Yes, I’m looking at you AQA. We’ve stopped our students understanding, participating in or belonging to the world of English.
But the curriculum is mainly what students do, not just what they read. How much of what they do is in the list above?
I can sum it up in one sentence: We no longer teach students to be students of English. They don’t master the subject, nor do they explore it. Is it any surprise they don’t enjoy it?
And this is because they don’t belong. English no longer makes them a better person. They are not part of a community of writers or readers. They don’t develop a voice that deserves to be heard.

Our students are homeless in the English classroom, because they have no foundations for a house. We just give them a random supply of bricks, we build an occasional wall and occasionally manage part of a roof. Sample this, compare that, annotate it and write me some more description.
What tasks would you set? Write them down, and stop when you have 10. How many of them look anything like the tasks students are set in your English curriculum?
